notes: Four of the planned sources are built, each as one module covering a family or a shape. The Archive-software family (Archive of Our Own and the archives running the same code) was written against four pages recorded from the live site on 2026-09-10. Royal Road was written against four more, and it is where the ported code was checked against the site and found wrong: published stored as 0 (the epoch, worse than an absent date), updated set to the moment of the fetch, the status hardcoded as ongoing for every work including completed ones, the author's profile URL left empty, each chapter keyed by its loop index rather than by the site's own chapter id, and the chapter title selected with `h2.chapter-title`, which matches nothing on the recorded page — a selector whose fallback titles every chapter "Chapter 1", "Chapter 2", discarding the author's titles with nothing raised. Syosetu was written against twelve pages covering three works, and is the first source that spreads one work over more than one page: its work page lists 100 episodes at a time and does not state how many a work has, so a preview that reads it once reports 100 of a 795-episode work and the import stores a seventh of it as a success. The adapter reads the info page first, walks every list page, and refuses when the two disagree. Its adult sibling host (novel18.syosetu.com) is deliberately not claimed: it is behind an age gate, so no page could be recorded to write a parser against, and a catalogue entry that always refuses is worse than an absent one. The eFiction family is the fourth, and the first adapter that is one module for nineteen archives across eighteen hosts rather than one module per site. It was written against the fourteen pages already reconnoitred and committed under tests/fixtures/efiction/ (five members), and it corrected two of that reconnaissance's own conclusions as well as the port's. The port's date table is a strftime list that cannot read either recorded member — `08/06/21` on tgstorytime and `January 18 2022` (no comma) on giantessworld both fail `%B %d, %Y` — so dates are parsed by shape, day-first for the numeric form with the two readings disambiguated against the future where they straddle it, and an unrecognised date is absent rather than guessed. The port's chapter keys were the loop index; the family's own key is the `chapid` on a chapter's review link, which a work page carries for every chapter without fetching one, and it is available on both members through different markup. A chapter has two URLs that are not two skins but the reading view (`&textsize=0&chapter=K`, prose in `div#story`) and the print view (`&chapter=K`, `printable.css`, `window.print()` on load) — and a table of contents links to the print view, so following the site's own links finds the wrong one; ninelivesarchive.com disallows the printable URL by name in its robots.txt. The adapter reads the reading view and falls back to the print view's container, and the fixtures assert the prose is byte-identical either way. Class values are read as the member rendered them — a `browse.php` link per value — rather than by splitting text, which is what keeps `Male to Female, Young Adult (20-26 yrs)` one value and `Slow/Gradual Change` unbroken; everything else a block contains is furniture, and reading it made tgstorytime's rating `Adult Download ePub`. Archive statistics and story metadata are told apart structurally, by container and by `Completed:`, because narutofic's statistics block carries `Chapters:` and `Word count:` too and reading it reports the archive's 25,318 chapters as one work's. Three outcomes that are not a story are distinguished rather than folded together: a moderation hold (`SourceError::Withheld`, new in this milestone — the work exists, the archive will not serve it, and calling it `NotFound` sends an operator looking for a typo), a content gate (`AuthRequired`, which pauses the job and is satisfied by a credential's `adult_allowed`), and a challenge wall (`Blocked`, matched on the interstitial's own markers rather than on the absence of content). The fixtures also exposed a crate-wide defect: every page in this family declares `charset=ISO-8859-1` and emits Windows-1252, and `String::from_utf8_lossy` in the fetcher turned every apostrophe into a replacement character, so a chapter title a reader would see was corrupted with nothing failing. Bodies are now decoded through `encoding_rs` by the declared charset with the WHATWG alias table — the same rule every browser applies — and the fix is in the fetcher, not in this adapter. Live verification reads giantessworld today (13 chapters, 27,507 words, complete) and the reading view's prose, and asserts that tgstorytime is refused by its own `Disallow: /` rather than read. What the family's reach actually is, of the eighteen hosts the adapter claims: nine are reachable, one (ninelivesarchive) permits the work page and forbids every chapter, two disallow the whole archive in robots.txt (tgstorytime, sinfuldreams), two answer Cloudflare 403, and four no longer resolve. Five tier-1 adapters remain (ffnet/fictionpress, the XenForo boards, scribblehub, wattpad, ficbook), and the rest of the ported adapters carry the same defects, so the remaining work is not a copy: each source needs real dates or none, the source's own chapter id, a title selector that matches, and sanitisation before its fixture test can pass. The port's member list is eighteen hosts; four names an earlier draft of the milestone plan carried (fanficauthors.net, lcfanfic.com, phoenixsong.net, mediaminer.org) appear in none of them and were invented. The four sources this row previously called unreachable because of a Cloudflare wall are no longer unreachable, and what changed is worth stating precisely. FanFiction.net, FictionPress, FimFiction and ScribbleHub refuse a plain client and serve a real page to a client whose TLS and HTTP/2 fingerprints are a browser's; FanFiction.net is now read live through the guarded fetcher (46,808 bytes of a real chapter, asserted together with the plain client's refusal, so the test cannot pass on a day the wall is switched off). The access path is crates/scrapers/src/engine.rs, a transport seam inside SafeFetcher rather than a second fetcher: the engine is the only thing that varies, so address pinning, hand-rolled redirects, the bounded read, the robots.txt gate and the pacing all stay in one place. Escalation runs only on a detected bot challenge, never on a 404, a robots.txt refusal or a rejected credential, and only for a strategy the adapter declared and the instance switched on. Both tiers were verified against a stub first and against real services second, and the second pass is where the mistakes were. Byparr 3.0.4 was installed and run: the live suite's new a_solver_passes_a_wall_a_fingerprint_does_not asserts, in order, that a plain client is refused, that a browser fingerprint is ALSO refused for FimFiction (three browsers, all refused there, against a FanFiction.net that accepts one - a fingerprint is a per-host fact, not a per-family one, and that is what the third tier exists for), that 241,315 bytes of the real story page come back through the solver, and that an undeclared host is still refused before any solve. The same fetcher reads FanFiction.net (48,743 bytes), FictionPress (35,740 - which the fingerprint could not touch at all), ScribbleHub (33,742) and SpaceBattles (1,526,890). Byparr's log shows what the tier buys: 'Challenge detected' then 'Clicked the challenge checkbox' twice, an interactive checkbox no header can set, costing about twelve seconds per page. Three bugs were found only because a real service was on the other end. (1) The endpoint was posted to as configured - 'http://127.0.0.1:8191' answers 405 Method Not Allowed, because that address serves the service's docs page and the contract posts to /v1; every stub test passed while this was broken, because a stub asserts on the body it is sent and never cared which path the body arrived at. The client now keeps a path the operator supplied and appends the versioned one to a bare address. (2) Byparr has no session API at all: the FlareSolverr v1 contract has one and the maintained successor dropped it, accepting a single LinkRequest{cmd, url, maxTimeout, blockMedia, returnOnlyCookies} over a browser it shares internally, with 'sessions', 'session' and 'cmd' appearing zero times in its source. The proactive sessions.create was parsed as a request for the empty URL and answered '502 Could not reach the target: ... Invalid url: https://'. Reads worked and only the log was wrong, but the operator's solver log filled with errors about a service that is working and every page paid for a wasted navigation. A session is now proven rather than assumed, and a one-page fetch never tries: the first request goes stateless, because a session exists to make later requests cheaper, and support is attempted only once a second request makes it worth having, then remembered either way. On FlareSolverr proper the session is still used. (3) The archive client let reqwest follow a redirect it had not checked - the real archive answers its entry URL with a 302 to the snapshot's own address, a hop that could leave the archive, in a crate whose premise is that an answer is not authority to request wherever it points. Redirects are now followed by hand with each hop checked against the archive's host, and provenance records the address actually read rather than the entry point. The archive tier's URL construction was checked against the real archive, which is reachable again (it answered 'temporarily offline' all of 2026-09-11 and now rate-limits this address with a 429): a missing snapshot is a 404 and a present one a 302, the two forms cannot be told apart by shape because the entry URL already carries the id_ modifier and still redirects, the bare-timestamp fallback correctly resolves to the newest snapshot (verified landing on 20260826131158), and id_ is the difference between a page and a wrapper around it measured rather than asserted - 636 kB wrapped against 93 kB raw. Whether a real snapshot of a real FFN chapter parses is still unverified, because no page of the recorded work has one and the tier needs an adapter to reach. The five tier-1 adapters still to write (ffnet/fictionpress, the XenForo boards, scribblehub, wattpad, ficbook) are now blocked on parsing rather than on access.

requirement: A shared safe fetcher: SSRF refused, rate limited, bounded
notes: Every byte an adapter reads goes through SafeFetcher, and an adapter cannot construct its own client — the trait hands it the fetcher, which is what makes the guard structural rather than advisory. Loopback, link-local, CGNAT, unique-local and metadata-service addresses are refused by name; a hostname is resolved and the answer checked, then pinned per request so a name cannot resolve to a public address for the check and a private one for the connection; redirects are followed by hand with every hop re-validated and the credential header stripped for any host but the source's own; bytes, time, redirect count and per-host concurrency are bounded while reading rather than after. Automatic decompression is off, so a decompression bomb cannot get in — and the file says so, because enabling that feature would quietly reopen it. Pacing and path rules come from the source rather than from this repository: the fetcher reads each host's robots.txt once per run and honours its Crawl-delay as the minimum gap, enforces its Disallow rules as refusals before any request is made, and falls back to one request per second where nothing is published — because no information is not no limit. A 404 means no restrictions; any other failure to read the file means the rules are unknown, so the import proceeds at the default pace and the condition is recorded rather than failing a reader's import over a file that is temporarily broken. The parser is a pure function over a string, so the whole policy is testable with no network (20 tests), and the match rule deliberately holds group names shorter than three characters to an exact match: our token 'Lorehaven' contains 'a', so the literal substring rule would let a stray 'User-agent: a' capture us and apply that group's rules silently.

requirement: Imported chapter bodies are sanitised before storage
notes: A chapter body is HTML written by a stranger, stored and then rendered, so it is sanitised on the way in by the adapter — the only code that knows which parts of a foreign page are prose. An allow-list of tags survives (paragraphs, breaks, emphasis, blockquote, lists, headings, ruby for CJK, hr); script, style, iframe, object, embed, form and img are dropped rather than escaped, because a reader's reader-version should not call out for tracking pixels it inherited from the source; every attribute is dropped except a link's href, which must be absolute http or https; entities are decoded and re-escaped, so text that already contains an entity does not come out over-escaped.

requirement: An import resumes: a retry re-reads only what failed
notes: A first import fetches the whole work in one request, because one request per work is what a source would rather receive. A retry reads the chapter record, skips what is stored, and asks the source only for the ordinals that failed — and only where the adapter advertises that it can address a chapter on its own, so a source that cannot is fetched in bulk with the skip rule doing the work. The test asserts *which ordinals were requested*, not how many rows exist at the end, because a retry that re-read the whole work would also finish with every chapter stored. A chapter that cannot be written does not discard the ones that could: it is recorded and the import fails at the end, so the queue retries what is left.

requirement: Source credentials are pseud-scoped, encrypted and never returned
notes: Milestone 5 shipped the encrypted store; this is its first real caller. A credential is scoped to the pseud that stored it, not the account, so one reader's login for a source cannot be used by another of their identities. Responses are built from a view type with no field for a secret, which is a stronger guarantee than remembering to skip one. The value is written before the row that names it, because source_credentials.secret_id is a foreign key and a credential whose value is missing is not a credential; the ciphertext is bound to the credential's natural key (pseud, source, label), so rotating a password replaces one secret row instead of accumulating orphans. Deleting a credential deletes the secret and lets the schema cascade take the row, so a revocation cannot leave a password behind because a caller forgot a second step; already-imported copies are untouched, as spec §11.6 requires. Storing a credential for a source that uses none is refused rather than stored and ignored.

requirement: Expired credentials pause affected jobs with an actionable status
notes: Checked before anything is fetched, so a stale login is a message rather than half an item in somebody's library. The refusal is fatal to the job rather than transient: retrying would send the same dead credential five more times, which spec §11.6 forbids. The message carries the expiry date, and the credential row is marked expired so the reader can see why without reading a log. The adapter is not called at all in either case.

requirement: Runtime source health states drive whether a source is used
evidence: crates/db/src/imports.rs::recompute_source_health + crates/app/src/routes/imports.rs (admin_router, refuse_unusable_source) + crates/app/src/worker.rs (sweep after every import) + crates/app/tests/milestone_6.rs (6 tests) + migrations/*/0006_imports.sql (sources.health)
notes: The catalogue reports each source's health, its last check, whether it is enabled and why not, and what its adapter can do — so capability absence is visible rather than discovered when an import fails (spec §11.1). The health column is now derived rather than left at unknown. A sweep recomputes it from the source's own finished imports over a seven-day window, and it runs after every import the worker carries out and on demand from POST /admin/sources/health, an operator route that answers 404 rather than 403 to anybody else — confirming that an operator surface exists is itself a disclosure. The rules are chosen so the state means something a reader can act on: one success and no failures is healthy; failures beside successes are degraded, because a source that usually works is not one to avoid; three failures with no success is unavailable; a cancellation counts as neither, because a reader who stopped an import has said something about the import and not about the source; and a source nobody has tried keeps what it had, because silence is not evidence. What the sweep will not do is what mattered most to get right: it never derives and never overwrites paused. A pause is an operator's decision, and a sweep that could clear one would silently re-enable a source somebody switched off on purpose while their reason sat on the row still looking current. The consequence of unavailable is that imports into it are refused before they are queued — at preview and at start — rather than queued and failed, which is the difference between an honest error and a promise the queue cannot keep; a source an operator paused is refused for the same reason, with the operator's own words in the message. What is still absent is the finer classification spec §11.8 sketches — outage, rate limiting, authentication failure, parser incompatibility, policy restriction, network failure, per-user access denial are classified in the error mapping the import uses but are not yet written back onto the source row, so a source cannot yet say *why* it is degraded.

A fetch may carry the validators the source gave last time (ETag, Last-Modified), and a 304 means the source has confirmed the revision we hold is current — so the reader is served the bytes already on disk and the body never crosses the network. The cache is a decorator rather than something each adapter opts into: every adapter already fetches through the Fetcher trait, so wrapping it means a new adapter gains conditional requests the moment it is registered, with nothing to remember. The key is four things and every one is load bearing — the source, the page, the adapter version and the security scope. The scope is the one that matters most: a page fetched with a reader's credential is a different resource from the same URL fetched anonymously, so a credentialed read is filed under the pseud it belongs to and never served to anybody else. The adapter version means a parser change stops the previous build's bytes being served as though this build had produced them. A page with no validators is not stored at all, because there would be nothing to ask about and the row would be a body nobody may serve. Nothing here may be mistaken for a snapshot: clearing the cache deletes entries and never touches content_blobs, which is shared with the chapters a reader is reading, and a test asserts exactly that. The cache is also never the reason a read fails — a missing blob, an unreadable row, a database error each degrade to an ordinary fetch with a log line. Writes get the fetch_cache retention class so the row explains itself. What is still absent is a scheduled re-read that would make the cache pay for itself across a whole library: the machinery is exercised by imports and previews, not yet by a periodic update check.
